text: nevertheless. Online courses are convenient. Nevertheless, they cannot replace the energy of a live seminar.
furthermore. The program reduces costs. Furthermore, it improves student satisfaction.
consequently. The library extended its hours. Consequently, more students studied on campus.
moreover. The policy saves money. Moreover, it protects the most vulnerable students.
nonetheless. The sample was small. Nonetheless, the findings were consistent with earlier research.
conversely. Cities with more green space report happier residents. Conversely, crowded districts show higher stress levels.
accordingly. The deadline was moved. Accordingly, the team adjusted its schedule.
subsequently. The university introduced free tutoring, and subsequently its pass rate rose by 12 percent.
hence. The data were incomplete; hence the cautious conclusion.
thus. The survey was anonymous; thus, honest responses were more likely.
cohesion. Transition words give an essay cohesion, linking each paragraph to the next.
signpost. Phrases like 'firstly' and 'in contrast' act as signposts for the reader.
seamless. The lecturer delivered a seamless argument from introduction to conclusion.
chronological. A chronological structure works best when you describe a sequence of events.
transition. The essay lacks transitions, so the reader struggles to follow the argument.
coherence. A strong outline gives an essay coherence from start to finish.
unity. Each paragraph should have unity: one main idea, fully developed.
elaborate. The professor asked her to elaborate on her second point.
outline. She wrote a quick outline before her timed essay.
emphasis. The course places emphasis on critical thinking rather than memorization.
reinforce. Examples reinforce the main argument by making it concrete.
relevant. Only include details that are relevant to your main claim.
concise. Concise sentences are easier to follow than long, tangled ones.
redundant. 'Free gift' is redundant because a gift is always free.
digress. The essay digresses into personal stories and loses its focus.
framework. The T-S-C framework keeps each paragraph on track.
hierarchy. A clear hierarchy of ideas helps readers see what matters most.
overarching. The overarching goal of the course is independent thinking.
embed. Embed one short example inside each paragraph to support your claim.
streamline. The university streamlined its application process.
ambiguous. The instructions were ambiguous, so students interpreted them differently.
explicit. The rubric makes explicit what examiners expect in each paragraph.
implicit. The author makes an implicit assumption that all readers share her values.
nuanced. Her nuanced answer acknowledged both sides before choosing one.
subtle. There is a subtle difference between confidence and arrogance.
precise. Use precise numbers: '47 percent' is stronger than 'many'.
vague. A vague thesis ('technology is bad') cannot be supported well.
inherent. There are inherent risks in relying on a single source of data.
arbitrary. The deadline felt arbitrary rather than connected to real learning goals.
unequivocal. The evidence provides unequivocal support for the new policy.
distortion. Selective statistics create a distortion of the real situation.
connotation. 'Cheap' and 'affordable' share a meaning but differ in connotation.
oversimplify. It would oversimplify the debate to blame only social media.
perpetuate. Publishing only successful studies perpetuates a distorted picture of science.
depict. The chart depicts the rise in renewable energy use since 2010.
substantiate. The author fails to substantiate her claim with data.
refute. New evidence refutes the earlier assumption that class size does not matter.
concede. I concede that online courses are flexible, but they lack real interaction.
compelling. She presented a compelling case for stricter emissions rules.
outweigh. The benefits of early intervention clearly outweigh the costs.
valid. Both sides make valid points about remote work.
credible. The study is credible because it used a large, random sample.
warrant. The results warrant further investigation.
undermine. Small inconsistencies undermine the credibility of the whole argument.
bolster. Additional data would bolster the author's conclusion.
counterargument. Address one counterargument to show your view is balanced.
assertion. The essay is full of assertions but lacks supporting evidence.
premise. The argument rests on the premise that students learn best in silence.
bias. The survey suffers from bias because only volunteers responded.
plausible. Her explanation is plausible, but it needs more evidence.
mitigate. Planting trees can mitigate the effects of urban heat.
exacerbate. Cutting public transport would exacerbate traffic congestion.
foster. Group projects foster collaboration and communication skills.
hinder. Constant notifications hinder students' ability to focus.
alleviate. Flexible deadlines alleviate stress during exam season.
deteriorate. Air quality deteriorated sharply after the new factory opened.
catalyst. The pandemic acted as a catalyst for online education.
ramifications. The decision had serious ramifications for rural communities.
inevitable. Some job displacement is inevitable as automation spreads.
detrimental. Sleep deprivation is detrimental to academic performance.
profound. AI has had a profound impact on how research is conducted.
trigger. A single viral post can trigger a wave of misinformation.
curtail. Budget cuts curtailed the university's research programs.
escalate. Without intervention, the dispute escalated rapidly.
unprecedented. The move to remote work was unprecedented in scale.
derive. The findings derive from three years of fieldwork.
indicate. The results indicate a clear link between sleep and memory.
constitute. Women constitute over half of the university's graduates.
assess. The study assesses the impact of class size on achievement.
interpret. Critics interpret the data differently.
attribute. She attributes the improvement to better teaching, not more tests.
correlate. Income strongly correlates with access to higher education.
comprise. The sample comprises 500 students from five countries.
illustrate. The graph illustrates the decline in newspaper readership.
examine. The essay examines both sides of the debate.
evaluate. We must evaluate whether the benefits justify the costs.
infer. From the passage, we can infer that the author doubts the policy.
demonstrate. The experiment demonstrates that the method works under pressure.
hypothesise. Researchers hypothesise that the effect fades after six months.
verify. Always verify statistics before citing them.
allocate. Allocate two minutes for planning before you start writing.
prioritise. When time runs out, prioritise the longest writing task.
sustain. Chunk-writing helps you sustain momentum for ten minutes.
deadline. The deadline for the scholarship application is Friday.
procrastinate. Students who procrastinate often rely on last-minute panic.
efficient. A five-sentence frame makes your writing more efficient.
tedious. Copying notes by hand is tedious, but it aids memory.
meticulous. Meticulous proofreading catches the spelling errors examiners notice.
methodical. Adopting a methodical approach prevents panic in the final minutes.
feasible. A shorter, focused essay is more feasible than a perfect one.
sufficient. One example is not sufficient to prove a general claim.
anticipate. Good test-takers anticipate difficult questions and stay calm.
contingency. Have a contingency plan if the recording fails.
sequence. The paragraph follows a clear sequence: point, example, comment.
compress. You must compress two ideas into one sentence here.
comprehensive. The report offers a comprehensive review of the research.
deliberate. Deliberate practice, not repetition, improves writing.
strategic. Strategic use of transitions improves your writing score.
systematic. Keep a systematic record of your recurring errors.
proactive. Being proactive about deadlines prevents last-minute panic.
recurring. Spelling under pressure is a recurring issue in timed essays.
proficiency. Students can demonstrate proficiency through real projects.
threshold. A score above the threshold guarantees an interview.
exemplify. Her essay exemplifies how a short response can still be persuasive.
ensure. Proofread to ensure that no spelling errors remain.
psychology. The psychology of decision-making fascinates behavioural economists.
useful. Feedback is most useful when it is specific.
source. Always cite a reliable source for statistics.
research. The research suggests that feedback improves performance.
paramount. In academic writing, clarity is paramount.
criterion. The most important criterion is whether the argument is supported by evidence.
merit. The proposal has real merit, but its cost is too high.
flaw. The study has one serious flaw: the sample was too small.
drawback. The main drawback of online study is the lack of direct contact.
advantage. Small classes have a clear advantage: students receive more feedback.
effective. The campaign was effective because it targeted a specific group.
adequate. The evidence is adequate to support the main claim.
satisfactory. The explanation was satisfactory, but it missed one important detail.
questionable. The conclusion is questionable because the data are incomplete.
defensible. Her position is defensible because she acknowledges the counterargument.
superior. The new system is superior to the old one in both speed and accuracy.
inferior. The cheaper material is inferior in durability, even if it looks similar.
inefficient. The approval process is inefficient because every decision needs three signatures.
validity. The validity of the survey depends on how the questions were worded.
assessment. The assessment rewards clarity as well as accuracy.
trend. The trend is clear: more students are choosing online courses.
increase. The number of applicants increased by 20 percent last year.
decrease. The dropout rate decreased after the tutoring program began.
plateau. Sales plateaued after the first year and stayed flat for a decade.
peak. Demand peaked in July before falling sharply in August.
fluctuate. Prices fluctuated throughout the year, with no clear long-term trend.
surge. There was a surge in applications after the fee was removed.
decline. Enrolment declined steadily for three years before recovering.
stabilize. The figures stabilized at around 60 percent after 2020.
marginal. The difference between the two groups was marginal and not significant.
substantial. The policy led to a substantial reduction in waiting times.
gradual. There was a gradual improvement in scores over the semester.
rapid. The rapid growth of the platform surprised even its creators.
proportional. The funding is proportional to the number of students enrolled.
trough. The economy reached its trough in 2009 and then began to recover.
whereas. The first study used interviews, whereas the second relied on surveys.
albeit. The policy was popular, albeit expensive to maintain.
despite. Despite the rain, the event attracted a large crowd.
notwithstanding. Notwithstanding the criticism, the project continued.
comparable. The two cities have comparable populations but very different transport systems.
distinct. The two groups have distinct needs and should not be treated alike.
disparity. The disparity between urban and rural schools remains wide.
resemble. The new design resembles the original, but the materials are cheaper.
diverge. The two approaches diverge sharply when costs are considered.
converge. The two estimates converge around 40 percent.
counterpart. The minister met her Japanese counterpart to discuss trade.
analogous. The heart is often described as analogous to a pump.
contrast. The report contrasts the two systems without recommending either.
parallel. There is a parallel between the two crises.
differentiate. It is hard to differentiate between the two products.
stem. The problem stems from a lack of clear communication.
arise. Difficulties arise when the instructions are unclear.
entail. The job entails working with international students.
precipitate. The scandal precipitated a crisis in the government.
provoke. The decision provoked widespread criticism.
spur. Tax breaks spurred investment in renewable energy.
curb. The city introduced new rules to curb traffic in the centre.
offset. Higher fuel costs were offset by lower rent.
amplify. Social media can amplify small errors into major scandals.
contribute. Several factors contributed to the decline in sales.
account. The report accounts for the difference in costs.
induce. The drug induces sleep within twenty minutes.
propagate. The internet propagates information faster than any previous medium.
constrain. A small budget constrained the scope of the study.
engender. Trust is engendered by consistent behaviour over time.
challenge. The biggest challenge is keeping the project on schedule.
obstacle. Cost is the main obstacle to wider adoption.
constraint. Time constraints forced the team to simplify the design.
remedy. There is no simple remedy for the housing shortage.
intervention. Early intervention improved outcomes for the children.
address. The report addresses the causes of youth unemployment.
tackle. The city is tackling air pollution with new transport rules.
resolve. The two sides resolved the dispute without going to court.
prevent. Vaccination prevents many serious diseases.
restore. The program aims to restore trust in local government.
sustainable. The city needs a sustainable transport system, not more roads.
viable. Solar power is now a viable alternative to coal in many regions.
implement. The school implemented the new policy in September.
combat. The campaign aims to combat misinformation online.
safeguard. New rules safeguard students' personal data.
methodology. The methodology section explains how the participants were selected.
sample. The sample included 200 students from five schools.
variable. The study controlled for age and income as variables.
empirical. The claim is supported by empirical evidence from three studies.
qualitative. The qualitative interviews revealed why students dropped out.
quantitative. The quantitative analysis showed a small but consistent effect.
reliability. The reliability of the test was checked by repeating it twice.
replicate. Other researchers failed to replicate the original findings.
findings. The findings suggest that early feedback improves retention.
questionnaire. The questionnaire asked students about their study habits.
longitudinal. The longitudinal study followed the same children for ten years.
dataset. The dataset contains responses from 5,000 households.
correlation. There is a strong correlation between attendance and grades.
generalize. It is risky to generalize from such a small sample.
scrutiny. The proposal came under close scrutiny from the committee.
curriculum. The curriculum now includes more practical projects.
pedagogy. The course combines technology with sound pedagogy.
feedback. Detailed feedback helped her improve the next draft.
retention. Regular review improves retention of new vocabulary.
engagement. Group projects increased engagement among quieter students.
autonomy. Online learning requires more autonomy than a traditional class.
misconception. A common misconception is that memorizing is always the best way to learn.
attainment. The gap in attainment between the two groups narrowed.
literacy. The program combines digital literacy with traditional reading skills.
numeracy. Employers increasingly expect basic numeracy as well as literacy.
vocational. Vocational courses prepare students for specific careers.
extracurricular. Extracurricular activities can develop leadership skills.
mentor. A mentor helped him choose which courses to take.
aptitude. She showed an aptitude for languages at an early age.
rote. Rote learning can help with facts but not with deep understanding.
enrolment. Enrolment in the online program doubled this year.
tuition. Tuition has risen faster than inflation for a decade.
scholarship. She won a scholarship that covers her full tuition.
dormitory. Most first-year students live in a dormitory on campus.
faculty. The faculty voted to change the assessment policy.
syllabus. The syllabus lists every reading and deadline for the term.
extension. He asked for an extension because he was ill.
registrar. The registrar confirmed that her transcript was ready.
transcript. The application requires an official transcript from each university.
prerequisite. Statistics is a prerequisite for the research methods course.
elective. She chose an elective in psychology outside her major.
seminar. The seminar was limited to fifteen students.
lecture. The lecture covered the causes of the French Revolution.
tutorial. The tutorial gave students time to ask questions about the assignment.
orientation. Orientation week helps new students find their way around campus.
productivity. Remote work increased productivity for some teams but reduced it for others.
incentive. Tax incentives encouraged companies to invest in clean energy.
remuneration. The job offers flexible hours but modest remuneration.
unemployment. Youth unemployment rose sharply after the recession.
inflation. Inflation reduced the real value of wages.
recession. The country entered a recession after two quarters of negative growth.
entrepreneurship. The university runs a program to encourage entrepreneurship among students.
workforce. Women make up nearly half of the workforce in the sector.
outsourcing. Outsourcing customer service reduced costs but damaged quality.
underemployment. Underemployment is common among graduates in the creative sector.
inequality. Income inequality has widened over the past decade.
mobility. Social mobility is lower in countries with expensive education.
expenditure. Public expenditure on health rose by five percent.
revenue. The company's revenue grew, but its profits fell.
subsidy. The subsidy made solar panels affordable for low-income families.
biodiversity. The forest supports an extraordinary level of biodiversity.
ecosystem. The river is part of a fragile ecosystem.
emission. Carbon emissions must fall sharply to meet the target.
renewable. Renewable energy now supplies a third of the country's electricity.
conservation. The conservation project restored the wetland habitat.
contamination. The contamination of the water supply was traced to a nearby factory.
depletion. The depletion of fish stocks threatens the local economy.
habitat. Urban expansion is destroying the habitat of many species.
climate. The climate in the region has become hotter and drier.
erosion. Coastal erosion has forced several families to move inland.
pollutant. The factory released a pollutant into the river.
recycle. The city recycles more than half of its household waste.
geothermal. Geothermal energy heats many homes in Iceland.
drought. The drought lasted three years and ruined the harvest.
extinction. The species is facing extinction because its habitat is disappearing.
algorithm. The algorithm decides which posts appear at the top of your feed.
digital. Digital tools have changed how students collaborate.
platform. The platform connects tutors with students around the world.
surveillance. Surveillance cameras have reduced theft in the city centre.
misinformation. Misinformation spread quickly during the election.
privacy. Users are worried about the privacy of their personal data.
innovation. The company invests heavily in innovation.
obsolete. The software became obsolete after the new system was introduced.
interface. The interface is simple enough for new users to understand.
network. The university network was down for two hours.
virtual. Virtual labs allow students to run experiments online.
immersive. The immersive exhibit made visitors feel part of the story.
curation. The curation of the exhibition took six months.
accessibility. Accessibility features help students with disabilities use the platform.
automation. Automation has replaced some routine jobs but created others.
wellbeing. Regular exercise improves both physical and mental wellbeing.
obesity. Childhood obesity has risen in many countries.
sedentary. A sedentary lifestyle increases the risk of heart disease.
nutrition. Good nutrition is essential for children's development.
epidemic. The epidemic overwhelmed hospitals in the region.
immunity. Vaccination builds immunity against the virus.
healthcare. Access to healthcare remains unequal in rural areas.
diagnosis. An early diagnosis greatly improves the chance of recovery.
prevention. Prevention is cheaper than treating the disease later.
addiction. Social media addiction can affect sleep and concentration.
stigma. The stigma around mental illness prevents many people from seeking help.
demographic. The demographic shift has increased demand for healthcare.
urbanisation. Rapid urbanisation has put pressure on housing and transport.
welfare. The welfare system supports families on low incomes.
sanitation. Better sanitation reduced the spread of disease.
